newsitem.title: UK: Majority gone, UK's Major enters terra incognita.
newsitem.headline: Majority gone, UK's Major enters terra incognita.

text.p: Britain's Conservative Prime Minister John Major this week enters a world unknown in British politics for 17 years, where the government cannot guarantee a majority in parliament.

It is territory familiar to most leaders Major met this weekend at a European Union summit in Dublin. For them, reliance on the support of smaller parties, whether via a coalition or an informal pact, is the norm.

In Britain, where a first-past-the-post electoral system rewards the biggest parties, a government reckons on getting its legislation through parliament simply by maintaining discipline among its own legislators.

But the triumph of the main opposition Labour Party in a by-election in Barnsley, northern England, last week means that 323 Conservative members of parliament now face exactly the same number of members representing opposition groups.
Already, the new arithmetic is imposing its logic on the politicians.

Barnsley's successful Labour candidate Jeff Ennis is hurrying to London on Monday to take his seat ahead of a vote on the government's negotiating stance in Europe on fisheries, which could bring a government defeat.
Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind has brought forward a trip to Cyprus so that he can be back for the 2200 GMT vote.
But even if Major's government loses this parliamentary vote, it does not have to call a general election.

In 1974, a Labour government came to power with an overall majority of just three seats, which soon disappeared because of by-election losses and the defection of two MPs. Major had a 21-seat majority at the last poll in 1992 but it has been whittled away by defections and by-election losses.
In 1974, Labour lost a series of major votes, including one which forced it to increase the prices British farmers were guaranteed for their produce.
Three years later, faced with certain defeat on a motion criticising his economic policy, then prime minister James Callaghan was forced to negotiate a pact with the Liberal Party and its 13 MPs.

The pact ended the following year and in 1979 the Conservatives carried a vote of no confidence in the government by a single vote, paving the way for a general election which took Margaret Thatcher to Downing Street.

Major is not yet in as parlous a condition as Callaghan was. For the time being, his government will retain its majority on the parliamentary committees which scrutinise government bills, so his legislative timetable should not be too disrupted.

But while Callaghan could turn to the Liberals, the party which now has 26 seats has said it would not dream of propping up the Conservatives before an election which must be called by May at the latest.
Major may therefore be forced into an informal arrangement with the nine Ulster Unionist MPs, whose prime political purpose is to retain British rule over Northern Ireland.
Some analysts doubt whether even their support will enable Major, whose party is 20 points behind Labour in opinion polls, to delay a general election until May.
Lord Tom McNally, who was head of Callaghan's political office in 1979, predicted the government could fall in early February.
"A formal motion of no confidence...will attract the minority parties who will have nothing to gain from propping up a dying Conservative administration," he said.
